label: Parliament
reason: The institution that SCORE chose for the test and that the Multi100 instruction of Task 2 named.
phrase: distrust of the national parliament
estimates: How much a respondent distrusts the national parliament, on the ESS trust scale of 0 to 10 turned round so that 10 means no trust at all.
explanation: The claim speaks of trust in politics, and the paper measures it with three institutions. SCORE tested the claim on the parliament column of Table 3, and the second Multi100 task told the analysts to focus on trust in parliament, so this is the outcome of the reference specification.

label: Politicians
reason: The second of the three outcomes of the paper, named in its abstract as trust in national politicians.
phrase: distrust of politicians
estimates: How much a respondent distrusts politicians, on the same reversed scale of 0 to 10.
explanation: The abstract of the paper speaks of "trust in national politicians and political institutions", and Table 3 reports a column for politicians. Distrust of politicians is higher on average than distrust of parliament, and the paper reads its association with concern about immigration as part of the same finding.

label: Legal system
reason: The third outcome of the paper, an unelected institution that it uses to argue that the effect reaches the political system as a whole.
phrase: distrust of the legal system
estimates: How much a respondent distrusts the legal system, on the same reversed scale of 0 to 10.
explanation: The paper calls the legal system "an unelected branch of the political system" and keeps it beside parliament and politicians on purpose: if concern about immigration goes with distrust of all three, the finding is less likely to be a verdict on the government of the day. It answers the claim in the broad sense of trust in the political system.

label: Mean of the three
reason: The mean of the three trust items, the composite that several analysts built in their first task.
phrase: the mean distrust of parliament, politicians and the legal system
estimates: The mean of the three reversed trust items, a scale of distrust in politics from 0 to 10.
explanation: The three items hang together closely, which is why several Multi100 analysts averaged them in their first task. The paper chose not to combine them, so that it could show the finding for each institution separately. A scale answers the claim about trust in politics as one construct, and with less measurement error than any single item.

label: Political parties
reason: The ESS asked about trust in political parties only from round 2, so the paper left the item out.
phrase: distrust of political parties
estimates: How much a respondent distrusts political parties.
explanation: Rounds 2 to 4 of the ESS also asked about political parties, but round 1 did not, so the paper left the item out to keep all four rounds (note 42). It would answer a related question on three rounds only, and the course extract does not carry it.

label: European Parliament
reason: The paper uses distrust of the European Parliament as a contrast: the claim is about national institutions.
phrase: distrust of the European Parliament
estimates: How much a respondent distrusts the European Parliament.
explanation: The paper reports that concern about immigration correlates far less with distrust of the European Parliament than with distrust of national institutions, and reads this as evidence that the association is not a general negativity. It serves the paper as a contrast for the claim and answers a different question.

label: No controls
reason: The association within each country-round without other controls, the claim as SCORE selected it, whose ellipsis drops the words about controls.
phrase: without other controls
estimates: The association between concern about immigration and distrust among respondents of the same country and round.
explanation: The sentence that SCORE selected begins with an ellipsis that removes "even after controlling for other predictors of trust in the political system", so as selected it asks only whether concern goes with distrust. Comparisons within each country-round already keep the countries apart, and this is the plainest answer to that reading.

label: Demographics
reason: Age, sex, education and household income, the demographic controls that the paper lists together.
phrase: holding age, sex, education and household income constant
estimates: The association holding constant age, sex, education and household income.
explanation: Older, less educated and poorer respondents tend both to worry more about immigration and to trust politics less, so these characteristics, which are settled before either attitude forms, are the least contested controls. Household income is missing for nearly a quarter of the respondents, so adding it also shrinks the sample.

label: Outlook and ideology
reason: Adds the controls that the paper uses against spuriousness: unhappiness, dissatisfaction with life, social contact, interpersonal distrust and left–right position.
phrase: holding constant the demographics, unhappiness, dissatisfaction with life, social contact, interpersonal distrust and left–right position
estimates: The association holding constant the demographics and the general outlook and ideology of the respondent.
explanation: The paper argues that a general pessimism, a sense of alienation or an ideology on the right could produce both concern about immigration and distrust of politics. These controls stand for that common cause, and they include unhappiness, which the Multi100 instruction of Task 2 required.

label: Controls of the paper
reason: The full set of individual controls of Table 3, which adds evaluations of the economy and of public services and the two vote controls.
phrase: holding constant the full set of controls of the paper
estimates: The association holding constant every individual control of Table 3 of the paper.
explanation: This is the adjustment of the paper and of the SCORE reproductions. It adds satisfaction with the economy, with household income and with health and education services, a vote for a cabinet party and a vote for a far-right party. Some of these may themselves follow from concern about immigration, or from distrust, so holding them constant can remove part of the association that the claim is about. The curve keeps the set because it defines the claim of the paper.

label: Paper without unhappiness
reason: The set of the paper without unhappiness, which the Multi100 instruction of Task 2 told the analysts to include; a check.
phrase: holding constant the controls of the paper except unhappiness
estimates: The association holding constant the controls of the paper apart from unhappiness.
explanation: Multi100 asked every analyst to keep unhappiness among the controls, and the paper rests its case against general pessimism partly on it. Leaving it out changes the estimate very little, which the course shows as a check.

label: Paper and satisfaction with the government
reason: Adds satisfaction with the government, as two analysts did, although it is close to the outcome itself.
phrase: holding constant the controls of the paper and satisfaction with the government
estimates: The association holding constant the controls of the paper and satisfaction with the way in which the government is doing its job.
explanation: Satisfaction with the government is an evaluation of the people in power, which is a large part of what distrust of parliament and politicians measures. Holding it constant compares respondents who already agree about the government, and so removes part of the association that the claim is about.

label: Country-level variables
reason: The country and country-round variables of the paper are constant within each country-round, so the fixed effects of the curve absorb them; a check in the multilevel model.
phrase: with the country-level variables of the paper as well
estimates: The association holding constant the far-right vote share, social protection spending, governance, GDP, unemployment and the history of immigration of the country.
explanation: These variables describe countries and rounds, not respondents. Once each country-round has its own intercept they cannot explain any difference between respondents of the same country-round, so they change nothing on the curve. They matter only in the multilevel model of the paper, which the course fits as a check.

label: No weights
reason: Every respondent counts once, as in the SCORE reproductions; the paper reports no weights.
phrase: each respondent counting once
estimates: The association in the pooled samples, each country-round counting by the number of its respondents.
explanation: Both SCORE reproductions fitted unweighted models, and the paper reports no weights. With comparisons within country-rounds, the estimate is an average of the associations in the country-rounds, in which larger samples and samples with more varied concern count for more.

label: Design weights
reason: The design weight corrects for unequal chances of selection within each country.
phrase: with design weights
estimates: The association in the population of each country, the country-rounds counting by the size of their samples.
explanation: Some national samples of the ESS give respondents unequal chances of selection, for instance by the size of their household. The design weight undoes that, so the estimate describes the adult population of each country rather than its sample.

label: Design and population weights
reason: Design weights multiplied by the population weight, so that each country counts by its adult population.
phrase: with design weights and population weights, so that each country counts by its population
estimates: The association among the adults of the 16 countries taken together, each country counting by its population.
explanation: The population weight of the ESS makes each country count by the size of its adult population, so that Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Spain dominate. This answers the claim for Western Europeans as one population, which is a different average from the one in which each national sample counts by its size.

label: Post-stratification weights
reason: The post-stratification weight of the ESS, which adds an adjustment for age, sex, education and region to the design weight; a check.
phrase: with post-stratification weights
estimates: The association in the population of each country, with the sample matched to population margins.
explanation: The ESS also supplies a post-stratification weight, which matches each national sample to population margins of age, sex, education and region, taken from the Labour Force Survey, on top of the design weight. It moves the estimate very little, so the course keeps it as a check.

label: Post-stratification and population weights
reason: Post-stratification weights multiplied by the population weight; a check of the population-weighted answer.
phrase: with post-stratification and population weights
estimates: The association among the adults of the 16 countries taken together, with each sample matched to population margins.
explanation: It combines the post-stratification and the population adjustments, and it gives an answer close to that of design and population weights together.

label: Non-minority citizens
reason: Citizens of the 16 countries who do not belong to an ethnic minority, as the paper defines its respondents.
phrase: among citizens of the 16 countries who do not belong to an ethnic minority
estimates: Every respondent of the 16 countries in rounds 1–4 who is a citizen and does not regard themselves as belonging to an ethnic minority.
explanation: The argument of the paper is about members of the national community who regard it as threatened by immigration, so it leaves out non-citizens and members of ethnic minorities (note 40). The course extract reproduces its count of respondents exactly, country by country.

label: All respondents
reason: Adds non-citizens and members of ethnic minorities, whose relation to the national community is part of the subject of the claim rather than its population.
phrase: among all respondents in the 16 countries
estimates: Every respondent of the 16 countries in rounds 1–4.
explanation: The paper reports that including these respondents changes its results very little, and the course confirms it. But the claim concerns the national community as its members understand it, so a population that includes immigrants answers a different question.

label: All countries of rounds 1–4
reason: Adds the countries of Central and Eastern Europe, where the paper argues that the immigration items measure something else.
phrase: among respondents in every country of rounds 1–4
estimates: The association across every country that took part in rounds 1–4.
explanation: The paper leaves out the newer democracies of Central and Eastern Europe, because there the questions about immigration are likely to be read as questions about conationals from neighbouring countries after border changes. Including them answers a question about a different set of societies, and the course extract holds only the 16 countries.

label: Index of three items
reason: The mean of the three immigration items, reversed so that high values mean concern, as the paper builds it.
phrase: concern about immigration, the mean of three items
estimates: Concern about immigration as the mean of three items on its effects on the economy, on cultural life and on the country as a place to live, from 0 to 10.
explanation: The paper averages the three items, which correlate strongly and form one scale in every country, so the index covers both the economic and the cultural concerns of the claim. A mean of several items measures the attitude with less error than any one of them.

label: Economy item
reason: One item of the index, on the economy: a narrower concern with more measurement error.
phrase: concern about the effect of immigration on the economy
estimates: Concern measured by the single item on whether immigration is bad or good for the economy.
explanation: The economic item captures one facet of the concern and carries more measurement error than the index, which pulls its coefficient towards zero. It answers the claim less well than the scale of the paper.

label: Cultural life item
reason: One item of the index, on cultural life: closest in wording to the national community, but a single item.
phrase: concern about the effect of immigration on cultural life
estimates: Concern measured by the single item on whether immigration undermines or enriches cultural life.
explanation: The item on cultural life is the closest in wording to concern about the national community, but as a single item it measures the attitude with more error than the index.

label: Place to live item
reason: One item of the index, on whether immigrants make the country a worse place to live, the measure of one analyst.
phrase: the view that immigration makes the country a worse place to live
estimates: Concern measured by the single item on whether immigration makes the country a worse or a better place to live.
explanation: One Multi100 analyst used this item alone. It is the most general of the three, but a single item carries more measurement error than the index, so its coefficient is smaller.

label: All items answered
reason: A scale counts only for respondents who answered every item, the focal rule of the SCORE reproduction osf.io/jp7tr.
phrase: counting a scale only for respondents who answered every item
estimates: Each scale (concern, interpersonal distrust and the mean of the trust items) is missing for a respondent who skipped any of its items.
explanation: Requiring every item keeps each scale on the same footing for every respondent. It is the focal rule of the SCORE reproduction osf.io/jp7tr, and it loses the respondents who skipped a single question.

label: Answered items
reason: A scale averages the items that were answered, the additional rule of the SCORE reproduction osf.io/jp7tr and the rule of the Multi100 file.
phrase: averaging whichever items of a scale were answered
estimates: Each scale is the mean of the items that the respondent answered.
explanation: Averaging the answered items keeps more respondents, at the price of scales that rest on fewer items for some of them. The SCORE reproduction osf.io/jp7tr reported it as its additional analysis, and the file that Multi100 gave the analysts was built this way.

label: Five ISCED levels
reason: Education in the five harmonised ISCED levels of the cumulative ESS file, entered as a number, as both SCORE reproductions did.
phrase: with education in five ISCED levels
estimates: Education entered as a number from 1 (less than lower secondary) to 5 (tertiary).
explanation: The cumulative ESS file holds education in five levels harmonised across countries. Both SCORE reproductions used this variable, and education is one control among many, so its coding matters little for the coefficient of concern.

label: Seven levels of the paper
reason: The seven-category scale that the paper describes is not in the cumulative ESS file.
phrase: with education in the seven levels of the paper
estimates: Education entered as a number from 0 (primary not completed) to 6 (second stage of tertiary).
explanation: The paper codes education from 0 to 6, the scale of the education question of the early rounds. The cumulative ESS file replaced it with the harmonised five-level variable, so the course cannot rebuild the coding of the paper exactly.

label: Cabinet and far-right votes
reason: A vote for a party in the cabinet on the day of the interview, and a vote for a far-right party of the appendix of the paper; non-voters count as neither.
phrase: with votes for a cabinet party and for a far-right party coded from the party lists, non-voters counting as neither
estimates: Two controls of the paper, built from the party for which the respondent voted at the last national election.
explanation: The paper codes as winners the respondents who voted for a party in government at the time of the survey, and as far-right voters those who voted for a party in its appendix list. The course follows both rules with the cabinets recorded by ParlGov and the party codes matched by Party Facts. Respondents who did not vote count as neither, as in both SCORE reproductions.

label: Non-voters left out
reason: Leaves out everyone who did not vote, about one respondent in six, by treating their vote controls as missing.
phrase: with the vote controls counted only for voters, so that non-voters are left out
estimates: The association among voters only.
explanation: Coding the vote controls as missing for non-voters drops about a sixth of the sample, and non-voters are among the most distrustful respondents. One SCORE reproduction first coded the controls this way and then changed its approach; the analysis answers the claim for voters only.

label: Largest party
reason: A vote for the party that came first at the last election, the coding of the file that Multi100 gave the analysts; a check.
phrase: with a vote for the party that won the last election
estimates: The winner control coded as a vote for the largest party of the last election rather than for a cabinet party.
explanation: The file that Multi100 gave the analysts codes as winners the voters for the single party that won the last election, which misses the junior partners of coalitions. The five analyses refitted on that file show how little this changes the coefficient of concern.

label: Complete cases
reason: Respondents with a missing answer on any variable of the specification are left out, as in both SCORE reproductions.
phrase: leaving out respondents with any missing answer
estimates: Every specification uses the respondents who answered all of its variables.
explanation: Leaving out incomplete cases is what a regression does by default. Each specification therefore has its own sample, which shrinks as controls with many missing answers, above all household income, are added.

label: Multiple imputation
reason: Fills in missing answers from the other variables, as the SCORE replication on round 5 did in an auxiliary analysis; a check.
phrase: with missing answers imputed
estimates: The association with missing answers filled in by multiple imputation.
explanation: Imputation keeps the respondents whom complete-case analysis drops, under the assumption that their missing answers can be predicted from what they did answer. The course teaches it as a check on the companion page, and it does not enter the curve.

label: As in the paper
reason: The paper reports 110,732 respondents in every model but does not say how it handled the answers that were missing.
phrase: with missing answers handled as in the paper
estimates: The association on all 110,732 respondents, as the tables of the paper report it.
explanation: The models of the paper report the full count of respondents, although several of its controls are missing for many of them; household income alone is missing for nearly a quarter of the respondents. The paper does not say how it filled the gaps, so the course cannot rebuild its sample, and both SCORE reproductions analysed about 69,000 respondents instead.

label: Country-round fixed effects
reason: Each country-round gets its own intercept, so respondents are compared only with others surveyed in the same country and round.
phrase: comparing respondents within each country-round
estimates: The association within country-rounds, averaged over them.
explanation: Concern about immigration is measured on respondents, so it varies inside each country-round. Fixed effects for country-round compare respondents surveyed in the same country at the same time, and so set aside every difference between countries and rounds, including all the country-level variables of the paper.

label: Country and round fixed effects
reason: An intercept for each country and a shift for each round, the structure of two analysts who added country dummies.
phrase: comparing respondents within each country, with a shift for each round
estimates: The association within countries, with the rounds allowed to differ by a common shift.
explanation: Country intercepts with round shifts keep countries apart but let a country change from round to round only as much as all countries do on average. Two analysts used country dummies with round effects, and the estimate differs very little from that with country-round intercepts.

label: Random intercepts
reason: The multilevel model of the paper, with random intercepts for country and country-round; at the reference settings it gives the coefficient of the fixed effects to four decimals, so it is a check.
phrase: a multilevel model with random intercepts for country and country-round
estimates: The association in a model that treats countries and country-rounds as draws from a population.
explanation: The paper fits a three-level model in HLM, and the SCORE reproductions fitted the same model with lme4. With hundreds of respondents in every country-round, its estimate of an individual-level coefficient is almost identical to the fixed-effects one, which the course shows as a check.

label: Pooled regression
reason: One regression without country effects, which mixes the differences between countries into the estimate.
phrase: one pooled regression without country effects
estimates: The association across all respondents, between and within countries at once.
explanation: Countries differ both in how concerned their citizens are about immigration and in how much they distrust politics, for reasons of their own history. A pooled regression mixes those between-country differences into the individual-level association, so it answers the claim less well than comparisons within countries.

label: Clustered by country
reason: Errors clustered by country, with t on 15 degrees of freedom, because respondents of one country share more than their round.
phrase: with errors clustered by country (16 clusters)
estimates: A two-sided test at the 5% level of the coefficient of concern, with errors that allow respondents of the same country to be alike.
explanation: Respondents of the same country share institutions, media and history across rounds, so the errors of the model are not independent. Clustering by country is the most cautious choice, and with only 16 clusters the test uses a t distribution on 15 degrees of freedom. Every specification of the curve passes it comfortably.

label: Clustered by country-round
reason: Errors clustered by country-round; stored for every specification as a check.
phrase: with errors clustered by country-round
estimates: The same test with clusters for each country-round.
explanation: Clustering by country-round treats the rounds of one country as independent, which gives smaller errors than clustering by country. The curve stores this test for every specification as a check.

label: Conventional errors
reason: Errors that treat every respondent as independent, which overstates the precision of a pooled cross-national sample.
phrase: with conventional errors that treat respondents as independent
estimates: The same test with errors that assume no similarity between respondents of the same country.
explanation: Conventional errors ignore that respondents of one country are alike, so at the reference specification they come out less than half as large as errors clustered by country, and across the curve between an eighth and three fifths as large. The course shows the conventional test as the instructive mistake.

label: Wild cluster bootstrap
reason: A wild cluster bootstrap by country, suited to few clusters; computed for the reference specification as a check.
phrase: with a wild cluster bootstrap by country
estimates: A test that multiplies the residuals of whole countries by random weights, with the null hypothesis imposed.
explanation: With few clusters, clustered errors can still be too small, and the wild cluster bootstrap is the usual remedy. At the reference specification it agrees with the clustered test, so the course reports it as a check rather than as the rule of the curve.

label: Points per point
reason: Points of distrust (0–10) per point of concern (0–10), the scale of the coefficient of 0.17 in the paper.
phrase: in points of distrust per point of concern
estimates: The change in distrust, on its scale of 0 to 10, that goes with one more point of concern about immigration.
explanation: The paper reports its coefficient on the original scales, 0.17 points of distrust in parliament per point of concern. Both scales run from 0 to 10, so the coefficient reads directly, and every point of the curve is placed on it.

label: Maximum effect
reason: Ten times the coefficient, the reading of 0.17 in the paper as "maximum effects of 1.7" across the whole scale of concern; a check.
phrase: as the difference across the whole scale of concern
estimates: The difference in distrust between the least and the most concerned respondents, ten times the coefficient.
explanation: The paper translates its coefficient into the difference between the two ends of the concern scale. It is the same estimate on a scale ten times as large.

label: Standardised coefficient
reason: The coefficient in standard deviations; a check.
phrase: as a standardised coefficient
estimates: The change in distrust, in standard deviations, that goes with one standard deviation of concern.
explanation: A standardised coefficient puts outcomes on different scales side by side. It depends on how varied concern and distrust are in the analysed sample, as well as on the association.

label: Partial correlation
reason: The scale on which Multi100 put every reanalysis, so that tests of different kinds can be compared.
phrase: as a partial correlation
estimates: The test statistic converted into a correlation by the rules of Multi100.
explanation: Multi100 converted each recorded test into a correlation, using the degrees of freedom of the test or, for a z statistic, the number of respondents. The curve stores the partial correlation of the conventional fit, which is the Multi100 value of a test on the degrees of freedom of the respondents.
